newsitem.title: USA: Green groups weigh in on U.S. electricity debate.
newsitem.headline: Green groups weigh in on U.S. electricity debate.

text.p: Environmental groups Thursday laid out their goals for opening power markets to competition, calling for a guaranteed 10 percent market share for renewable fuels in power generation by 2010.
The 28 groups, including consumer advocates, called for new caps on power plant emissions, a fee to fund programs for low-income households and energy conservation and renewable energy technologies.
They also said they opposed outright repeal of the Public Utility Holding Company Act, a law designed to limit multistate utilities' investments in unrelated businesses.
The coalition said it had yet to find someone in Congress to push its views in the debate over how to move to an open market for power supplies to all consumers.
"We put together our ideas, now we need to find a champion on the Hill," said Charlie Higley, a coalition spokesman and senior policy analyst for consumer group Public Citizen.

The renewable energy standard the green groups sought was more than double the level proposed in a sweeping bill by Rep. Dan Schaefer, R-Colo., But their standard was lower than proposed by Sen. Dale Bumpers, D-Ark., who included hydropower in his plan.

Unlike the coalition, Bumpers and Schaefer proposed to repeal the utility holding company act, a law which securities regulators say is obsolete because the safeguards it provides are duplicated by state and federal utility commissions.

The green groups' agenda was notably silent about concerns which have been raised by Northeastern states that electric competition might spur coal-fired power plants in the Midwest to step up their output and blow more smog into the Northeast.
"The pollution impact is very controversial," Higley said. "We're not sure whether we're calling for the Clean Air Act to reopened. That may be something we ask for down the road."

Taking a more proactive stance, Rep. Frank Pallone, D-N.J., plans to reintroduce legislation he offered last year, that would require Congress to tighten the Clean Air Act before it unleashes competition among power producers.
But Higley said reopening the clean air law might not be necessary if the Environmental Protection Agency has the power to prevent increases in pollution from power plants.

To find out exactly what authority EPA has, Democratic Reps. Ed Markey of Massachusetts and Henry Waxman of California recently asked the agency to spell out its views on the environmental impact of power market competition and the extent of EPA's authority to tackle any potential harm.
Markey said Wednesday there should be "no net increase in pollution" as a result of electricity market changes.
